content: If the placenta cannot be removed, the woman should be referred to a hospital immediately. During the transfer, establish an intravenous (IV) line and administer fluids containing 20 IU of oxytocin at a rate of 30 drops per minute. Avoid applying excessive traction on the umbilical cord and do not squeeze or push the uterus to deliver the placenta. Once the placenta is delivered, ensure that it and the membranes are complete. If the placenta is incomplete, manually remove any retained fragments. During the third stage of labor, ensure the uterus is well-contracted and monitor for heavy bleeding. If heavy bleeding occurs, massage the uterus to expel clots until it becomes firm, administer 10 IU of oxytocin intramuscularly, call for assistance, start an IV line with 20 IU of oxytocin in fluids at 60 drops per minute, and empty the bladder. If bleeding persists and the uterus remains soft, continue massaging the uterus, apply bimanual or aortic compression, maintain IV fluids with oxytocin, and urgently refer the woman to a hospital. For third-degree tears involving the rectum or anus, refer the woman urgently to a hospital. For other tears, apply pressure with a sterile pad or gauze, bring the legs together, and reassess after five minutes. If bleeding continues, repair the tear or refer to a hospital. Collect, estimate, and record blood loss throughout the third stage of labor and immediately afterward. If blood loss is approximately 250 mL but bleeding has stopped, plan to keep the woman under observation for 24 hours, monitoring her intensively every 30 minutes for the first four hours. If observation at the facility is not possible, refer her to a hospital. Clean the woman and the area beneath her, place a sanitary pad or clean cloth under her buttocks to collect blood, and assist her in changing clothes if necessary. Keep the mother and baby in the delivery room for at least one hour after the placenta is delivered. Dispose of the placenta safely and appropriately, using gloves and a leak-proof container. If the fetal heart rate (FHR) is less than 120 or greater than 160 beats per minute, position the woman on her left side. If the membranes have ruptured, check for a prolapsed cord and assess the color of the amniotic fluid for meconium staining. Repeat the FHR count after 15 minutes. If a prolapsed cord is visible or palpable, manage the situation urgently. If the baby is not well during early labor, refer the woman urgently to a hospital and keep her lying on her left side. If the baby is not well during late labor, call for help, monitor after every contraction, and prepare for newborn resuscitation if necessary. For breech presentations, confirm full cervical dilation, ensure the bladder is empty, and prepare for newborn resuscitation. Assist the woman into a position that allows the baby to hang down during delivery. Perform an episiotomy if needed and allow the baby’s buttocks, trunk, and shoulders to deliver spontaneously during contractions. If the head does not deliver after several contractions, use gentle techniques to aid delivery, such as applying pressure to the baby’s cheekbones to flex the head. If the arms or shoulders are trapped, gently guide the baby’s body to release the arms. If the head is trapped and the baby is deceased, tie a weight to the baby’s feet and await full cervical dilation before proceeding with delivery. For multiple births, prepare the delivery room and equipment for the birth of two or more babies, including warm cloths, cord ties, and resuscitation equipment. Deliver the first baby following standard procedures, label them as Twin 1, and have a helper attend to the baby. Palpate the uterus to determine the lie of the second baby and adjust the presentation if necessary. Await strong contractions and spontaneous rupture of the second amniotic sac. Deliver the second baby, label them as Twin 2, and check for a third baby. Do not attempt to deliver the placenta until all babies are born, and do not administer oxytocin until after the final birth. After delivery, administer 10 IU of oxytocin intramuscularly once it is confirmed that no additional babies are present. Deliver the placenta and membranes by applying traction to all cords together. Monitor closely for vaginal bleeding, as the risk of postpartum hemorrhage is higher. Examine the placenta and membranes for completeness. Provide immediate postpartum care, including monitoring for bleeding, ensuring the mother and baby remain together, and offering support for feeding and care of the babies. Within the first hour after delivery of the placenta, assess the mother and newborn for any complications. Monitor the mother’s vaginal bleeding, encourage her to eat and drink, and ensure she has someone to stay with her. For the newborn, wipe the eyes, apply antimicrobial drops or ointment, and avoid washing it away. Do not bathe the baby or remove vernix. Keep the baby warm through skin-to-skin contact and encourage breastfeeding when the baby shows readiness. If the baby has difficulty breathing or is cold, take appropriate measures to address these issues. If the baby is stillborn or deceased, provide supportive care to the mother and her family. Continue monitoring the mother and baby intensively for the first few hours after delivery, ensuring they are not left alone. Do not discharge the mother before 24 hours, and provide advice on postpartum care and hygiene. Encourage the mother to eat, drink, and rest, and ensure she has access to sanitary materials for vaginal bleeding.
